description: We're looking for teammates with skills in Python, data analysis, physics, astronomy, orbital mechanics, and scientific modelling. Experience with web development, frontend design, data visualization, GIS, or 3D visualization would also be valuable. You don't need to be an expert in every area—curiosity, collaboration, and a willingness to learn are just as important. We'd be glad to work together!
summary:
SPHERExView is an open-source, web-based time-domain astronomical image explorer built for the NASA Space Apps Challenge (Planet X and SPHEREx). Inspired by Backyard Worlds' WiseView, it lets researchers and citizen scientists enter any object name or ICRS sky coordinate (RA/Dec) to blink multi-epoch infrared cutouts across NASA's 2025–2027 SPHEREx survey passes (DR1 & QR3), inspect a 5-epoch × 6-detector (30-image) wavelength matrix (0.75–5.00 µm), and extract calibrated 102-channel spectra on the fly.

Unlike naive image viewers that compare raw pixel grids or plot noise on empty sky, SPHERExView propagates proper motion from J2000/J2016 to the observation epoch before querying NASA/IPAC IRSA, reprojects frames onto a common gnomonic (TAN) WCS grid, subtracts zodiacal light (ZODI), and signal-gates spectral extraction at ≥3.0σ. Every clicked or auto-spotted moving candidate is cross-checked live against Gaia DR3, AllWISE, 2MASS, SIMBAD, and JPL SBIdent—preventing false-discovery alerts on already-cataloged objects.
details:
What does it do & how does it work? Users enter any star, brown dwarf, galaxy, or RA/Dec coordinate. The Python FastAPI backend (or browser-direct VO fallback) resolves the target viaCDS SesameandJPL Horizons, propagates proper motion to the 2025–2026 SPHEREx survey epoch, and queriesNASA/IPAC IRSA TAP & SIAv2(spherex.artifact, spherex.obscore, spherex_dr1, spherex_qr3). Astropy and reproject align cutouts onto a common TAN WCS grid (6.2″/px), subtract HDU 4 ZODI, and render synchronized single-band blink/difference/shift-and-add viewports alongside a 5×6 (30-tile) epoch-by-band matrix. Clicking any ≥3.0σ source extracts its 102-band spectrum (auto-scaled in µJy, mJy, or Jy) and multi-epoch light curve while verifying it against Gaia DR3, AllWISE, 2MASS, SIMBAD, and JPL SBIdent.

Benefits & Intended Impact SPHERExView lowers the technical barrier to exploring 7-extension SPHEREx FITS files (IMAGE, FLAGS, VARIANCE, ZODI, EPSF, WCS-WAVE) while enforcing strict scientific honesty: known stars are immediately labeled as cataloged, unresolved binaries (such as ε Indi Ba/Bb at 0.73″) are disclosed at 6.2″/px, and distant solar system candidates (like Sedna at 82.76 AU) return statistical-ranging orbit families rather than overclaimed unique orbits.

Tools, Languages & Software Used

  • Backend: Python 3.11, FastAPI, Uvicorn, Astropy, reproject, photutils, SciPy, NumPy, Pillow, httpx, astroquery, pyvo
  • Frontend: HTML5 Canvas, Vanilla JavaScript, Tailwind CSS, Chart.js
  • Hosting & Testing: Render Web Service (uvicorn main:app), unittest (7-test astrometric & photometric suite)

Creativity & Factors Considered Combining WiseView's intuitive blink/invert/stretch workflow with SPHEREx's 102-channel spectroscopy in a single dual-viewport + 30-tile matrix makes faint infrared movers (WISE 0855) and variable stars (RW Aurigae, R Draconis) immediately intuitive. Key engineering factors included cos(δ) spherical separation accuracy at high declinations, epoch-compensated cutouts for fast movers (Barnard's Star), zero-offset zoom/pan click-to-WCS mapping, and graceful degradation between server-side IRSA FITS processing and browser-direct VO queries.
